title: Listening in Mali Gaura
hook: listen to one hymn and its Bhagat verse

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mali Gaura, and your line was short and sweet. What did you say in fewer words, and what happened after you stopped? Day one thousand one hundred five.

Blessed is the wool. That's a line from the Guru Granth Sahib. Not blessed is the temple, not blessed is the king. Blessed is the wool, and the blanket made from it. It comes near the end of Mali Gaura, in the first hymn of the guest we met yesterday, Bhagat Namdev. Today we read along with him, slowly, the way the practice asks, and find out why a saint would bless a sheep's coat.
screen: `BLESSED IS THE WOOL.` → `THE GUEST AT THE END.` → `READ ALONG WITH NAMDEV.`

segments.voice: Namdev's hymn starts with music. Given here in plain English, not word for word: blessed, blessed is that flute the Lord plays; the sweet, sweet sound rings out, unstruck. That line is marked Rahao, pause, and in Sikh reading the Rahao line is treated as the center the rest of the hymn turns around. So hold onto it: sweet, sweet. Then Namdev starts blessing things. Blessed is the wool of the sheep. Blessed is the blanket Krishna wraps around himself. Blessed is mother Devaki, in whose home the Lord was born. Blessed is the forest of Brindaban. Namdev is singing from inside the stories of his own world, the cowherd Krishna with his flute, and Sikhs read these names as names for the one God the whole Granth praises. Read along and watch the direction. Namdev doesn't stay with the grand things. He goes to the wool. The blanket. A mother's house. A forest. The holy, in this hymn, makes everything near it holy too: the ordinary cloth, the ordinary home. It's a short hymn, and you can hear it end to end in one sitting. That's why the practice is to read along: with the words in front of you, the blessings stack up one by one, and you can see the hymn walking outward from the flute to the wool. In Gurmukhi, the word for sweet here is madhur, and Namdev doubles it, madhur madhur. Short, and doubly sweet. So yesterday's line turns around. Mali Gaura was short and sweet. Namdev's verse is sweet and short.
screen: `THE FLUTE: SWEET, SWEET.` · `RAHAO: THE CENTER LINE.` · `BLESSED IS THE WOOL.` · `FROM THE FLUTE OUT TO THE BLANKET.` · then, large: `SWEET AND SHORT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless what's near. Sit, and let your eyes rest on whatever is closest. A sleeve. A cup. The chair. Namdev blessed wool and a blanket; you can simply notice one ordinary thing with care. Where did it come from? Whose hands touched it before yours? Let it be quietly important for a minute. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you look at it. If you don't, just keep your attention on it, gently. Later today, find Namdev's hymn in Mali Gaura, open the words with a translation, and read along as it's sung. The bell holds the time.
Listening in Mali Gaura. Reading along with Bhagat Namdev's verse: the flute's sweet, sweet sound, and blessings on the wool and the blanket. Today's word.
Your line: sweet and short. Once today, pick up one ordinary thing, a scarf, a mug, a pen, and give it one sentence of thanks in your head. Day one thousand one hundred five.

howItsDone: Hymns of the Bhagats, like Namdev's, are sung in kirtan in their raga just as the Gurus' hymns are, and many listeners follow the Gurmukhi text with a translation on a screen or in a book while it is sung.
